claims.claim: Node handles thousands of concurrent sockets on one process without trouble.
claims.measured: I/O wait test at 256 connections only: node-express 14,188 req/s, p99 35.39 ms, 68 MB; node-fastify 17,462 req/s, p99 27.96 ms, 69 MB
claims.why: The highest concurrency measured is 256 connections, so the measurements can't confirm or refute behaviour with thousands of open sockets.

claims.claim: Go would also work, but the gain doesn't justify a second language (i.e. Go's advantage over Node for this workload is modest).
claims.measured: I/O wait: go-gin 20,235 req/s, go-nethttp 18,905 req/s vs node-fastify 17,462 req/s, node-express 14,188 req/s
claims.why: On the I/O-wait workload Go is only about 1.1–1.4x faster than Node, which fits the claim that the gain is small.

claims.claim: Go: low memory per in-flight request.
claims.measured: I/O wait peak memory at 256 connections: go-gin 16 MB, go-nethttp 15 MB vs node-express 68 MB, node-fastify 69 MB
claims.why: With 256 concurrent waiting requests, Go peaked at roughly a quarter of Node's memory, so it does use little memory per in-flight request.

claims.claim: At 500 in-flight deliveries and 1 s average latency, one process handles about 500 deliveries/s.
claims.why: This is Little's-law arithmetic about outbound calls with 1 s latency at 500 concurrency, and no measurement covers that level of concurrency or that kind of outbound client work.

claims.claim: The worker is I/O-bound, so compute should stay small.
claims.measured: I/O wait (10 ms per request): node-express 14,188 req/s at 92% CPU, node-fastify 17,462 req/s at 76% CPU on 1 CPU
claims.why: Node served about 14–17k waiting requests/s on one core, so about 2,500/s at peak would need only a fraction of a core, though outbound TLS client calls weren't measured.
